passage:
Dear Manoj,
Thanks for Thursday. When you said I looked like a phone at two percent, I did my usual thing and made a joke about being "fine, just caffeinated." You didn't laugh, you just said, "Rest, Dhruv." I went home angry at how right you were. Then you turned up on Saturday with parathas and dragged me on that slow walk along the canal, and I finally admitted how tired I've been. I let you carry the plates. It felt strange to be looked after, but I slept properly for the first time in weeks. Next Saturday I'll bring the tea. Thank you for not letting me joke my way out of it 🙂
Dhruv

qa.q: What did Manoj bring on Saturday?
qa.a: Manoj brought parathas.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv go home angry after Manoj's remark?
qa.a: Dhruv had joked about being "fine, just caffeinated" to hide the tiredness, and Manoj's plain "Rest, Dhruv" showed how right the concern was.

qa.q: Which small acts helped Dhruv begin to recover?
qa.a: The slow walk along the canal, the shared meal, letting Manoj carry the plates and finally sleeping properly.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt when Dhruv answered with a joke?
qa.a: Probably worried, since Manoj did not laugh and repeated the advice to rest instead of letting it slide.

grounding: A friend notices exhaustion and says to rest; the person stops joking it away and accepts a walk and a shared meal as part of recovery.

passage: For months I told myself I was just tired. I woke in the small hours, skipped lunches and couldn't enjoy anything, but I felt weak for even thinking about seeing someone. Finally I booked a session with Tanuja, a therapist, and sat in the waiting room rehearsing excuses. Instead I told her everything: the scrolling until dawn, the endless coffees, how I'd stopped calling my friends. She didn't look shocked. She wrote things down, asked gentle questions, and explained what we could try together. Walking out, I noticed something loosen in my chest. Later, two colleagues admitted they were seeing counsellors too. It seems many of us are learning that asking for help is normal, even a sign of strength. — Nikita

qa.q: Who did Nikita book a session with?
qa.a: Nikita booked a session with Tanuja, a therapist.

qa.q: Why did Nikita feel weak about seeing someone?
qa.a: Nikita believed needing help meant being weak, which is why Nikita sat in the waiting room rehearsing excuses.

qa.q: Why did being honest with Tanuja matter?
qa.a: Telling everything about the sleep, the coffees and the friends gave a fuller picture, which allows better care.

qa.q: How might the two colleagues have felt when they admitted seeing counsellors too?
qa.a: Perhaps relieved to say it aloud. Sharing it helps show that seeking help is normal.

grounding: Finally seeking help for exhaustion and low mood: honesty about symptoms and habits allows better care, and seeking help is strength.

passage: Ganga had wanted to teach in her hometown school since she was twelve, and for two years it felt like a dream. Now the mornings tasted like chalk dust. She marked the same copies, filled the same registers, and felt nothing. "Maybe I chose wrong," she told Farhan, the head teacher, over tea at the school gate. "Which part still makes you feel something?" he asked. She thought. "The reading circle. When a child finally gets a word." "And what are you avoiding?" "The staff meetings. And the endless forms." They looked at the timetable together. By the next month Ganga ran the library corner two afternoons a week, and Farhan had taken the forms off her desk. She still had bad days. But she no longer wanted to leave everything.

qa.q: Which part of teaching still made Ganga feel something?
qa.a: The reading circle, when a child finally gets a word.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling about her career when she spoke at the school gate?
qa.a: She felt empty and doubted her choice, as shown by "Maybe I chose wrong" after two years of a dream.

qa.q: What changed in Ganga's routine, and why is that a sensible kind of change?
qa.a: She got the library corner and lost the forms. Adjusting a role and rhythm addressed what she avoided without abandoning everything.

qa.q: How does Farhan approach Ganga's doubts?
qa.a: He asks what still matters and what she avoids, then adjusts the timetable, rather than telling her to leave or to just cope.

grounding: Dream career feels empty after novelty ends; asking what still matters and what is avoided, and changing a role or rhythm rather than everything.

passage: Sabina, I'll tell you about the winter I turned twenty-five, when my friend Anil died. He was twenty-six. I, Karthik, didn't believe it until I stood at the rites, and even then my hands felt like someone else's. For a week I buried myself in work and told everyone I was fine. It didn't hold. One night I heard his laugh in an old voice note and finally cried on the office stairs. After that I did things properly. I went to his family's house and sat with his mother, and we swapped stories about him until we were both laughing and crying. I checked on them every month. Some days I still feel unsafe, but the grief stopped being a wall and became a room I can enter.

qa.q: How old was Anil when he died?
qa.a: Anil was twenty-six.

qa.q: Why did Karthik keep telling everyone "I'm fine" while burying himself in work?
qa.a: Karthik was avoiding the grief and trying to numb it, but it did not hold, and it broke through at the sound of Anil's laugh in the voice note.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that helped both Karthik and Anil's family?
qa.a: Karthik attended the rites, cried, swapped stories with Anil's mother and checked on the family every month.

qa.q: How might Anil's mother have felt when Karthik visited and shared stories?
qa.a: Probably comforted, not alone in remembering her son, laughing and crying together. 🤍

grounding: A friend dies young; grief is allowed to be messy, with rites, stories, tears and checking on the family instead of numbing with work.

passage: Noor, come sit, and let me tell you something I've told very few. I, Hafsa, was twenty-five and sitting exams in another city when my Dada died. I'd missed his last three calls because I was studying. For a long time I carried that like a stone. I thought guilt meant I had failed him. Then a friend said, gently, that guilt can be love with nowhere to go. So I said everything aloud to that friend, all I was ashamed of. I also wrote Dada a letter, all the things I'd have said on those calls, and read it out beside his photograph. It didn't end the missing. But I began visiting his old friends, I cook his rice pudding every year, and I always pick up when someone I love calls.

qa.q: What was Hafsa doing when Dada died?
qa.a: Hafsa was sitting exams in another city.

qa.q: What did Hafsa first believe the guilt meant?
qa.a: Hafsa believed it meant having failed Dada, which is why it felt like a heavy stone.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do about the guilt, and how does Hafsa honour Dada now?
qa.a: Hafsa said it aloud to a friend and wrote Dada a letter, then visits Dada's old friends, cooks his rice pudding and answers calls from loved ones.

qa.q: What might have stayed the same for Hafsa if the guilt had never been spoken aloud?
qa.a: The stone would probably still be carried alone, with the belief that guilt meant failure instead of love.

grounding: Guilt over being away or busy when a grandparent died; speaking it aloud, writing what would have been said, and honouring them by how one lives.

passage: I'm Rekha, Simran's cousin, and I was in the hall the night the uncles began to argue. Simran's father had died five days before. One uncle wanted the rites done his way, another accused him of not being there in the last months, and then someone mentioned the house. Voices climbed. Simran stood up, pale, and said, "Everyone in this room is hurting. Please, no papers, no property, not now." The room went quiet. I couldn't tell if Simran was angry or just too tired to shout. After a pause Simran asked Bade Mama, the eldest, to help settle the rites, and said the house could wait until the family had rested, with someone neutral present. Nobody thanked Simran, but nobody argued again that night.

qa.q: How many days before the argument had Simran's father died?
qa.a: He had died five days before.

qa.q: What might Simran have been feeling when standing up, pale, to speak?
qa.a: Simran was probably hurt and worn out, and wanted to protect the family. Rekha admits it is hard to tell whether it was anger or tiredness.

qa.q: What else can the family do to keep Simran's father's memory from becoming a battlefield?
qa.a: Leave property and legal talk until everyone has rested, and rely on the eldest or a neutral person to help settle disputes.

qa.q: How might the uncles have felt during the argument?
qa.a: Probably grief, coming out as blame and demands. Simran's words, "Everyone in this room is hurting," point to that.

grounding: Grief sparks fights among relatives over rituals, property and blame; remembering all are hurting, delaying legal talk and involving elders or a neutral person.

passage: You brought that tiffin and didn't say a word, Hansa. I remember the steel lid clinking on my table. I'm Santosh, the one who always has a joke, and after Baba died I had none. Every relative who came had a sentence ready. You just sat. I ate half a roti and you didn't comment. That silence was the kindest thing anyone gave me that week. But by the third week the house had gone quiet, people had gone back to their lives, and I felt the drop. So I told you plainly: "Could you come for a walk on Sundays, and could you say his name sometimes?" You said yes, and you did. I'd never have guessed that asking would be the hard part, but it changed everything.

qa.q: What did Hansa bring to Santosh's house?
qa.a: Hansa brought a tiffin.

qa.q: Why did Hansa's silence feel kind to Santosh?
qa.a: Santosh could not speak, and relatives kept offering ready sentences. Hansa offered steady presence instead of words.

qa.q: What did Santosh ask for in the weeks after, and why then?
qa.a: A Sunday walk and to hear Baba's name sometimes, because by the third week the house went quiet and support had faded.

qa.q: How might Hansa have seen Santosh's request?
qa.a: Probably as welcome and clear, since Hansa said yes and kept doing it. Knowing what to do can be easier than guessing. 🤍

grounding: Friends bring food and sit silently; the grieving person accepts and, since support fades, says what is needed in the weeks after.

passage:
Dear Dhruv,
It's three weeks since Nani left us, and I'm still holding on to the small things. Each dawn I sit with her prayer book and read the verses she loved, even when the words blur. The evening lamp, the neighbours singing softly, the smell of incense, they hold me when reasoning can't. I'm not asking the pain to vanish; I only ask for steadiness. Some nights, though, I'm angry, and I wonder if anyone is listening. I've never said that aloud before, and I'm saying it to you because you won't flinch. Please don't fix it. Just read this and tell me if you've ever felt the same.
Yogesh

qa.q: What does Yogesh read each dawn?
qa.a: Yogesh reads the verses Nani loved from her prayer book.

qa.q: Why does Yogesh say "I'm not asking the pain to vanish"?
qa.a: Yogesh wants steadiness and comfort while grieving, not for the loss to be erased.

qa.q: What could Dhruv do in reply?
qa.a: Listen without trying to fix it, share honestly if Dhruv has felt something similar, and let Yogesh keep speaking about the doubts.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel on receiving this letter?
qa.a: Probably trusted and moved, perhaps unsure what to say. Yogesh's line "you won't flinch" shows how much that trust means.

grounding: Rituals, prayer and scripture hold the mourner when reason cannot; comfort without demanding pain vanish, and shaken faith spoken to a trusted person.

passage: Counsellor's note, Zubin. Ritu came in ten days after her brother's funeral, worried that something was wrong with her. "I feel nothing," she said. "Everyone else cries and I just make tea." She sat very straight with her hands in her lap and hadn't looked up once. I told her that going numb is very usual in the first days and does not mean she didn't love him. I asked what she had been doing each day, and it turned out she was still going to work, eating, and washing up, which is exactly what helps. We agreed she would keep those routines and let feelings arrive when they arrive. I suggested she come back next week, and said that if the heaviness stays for a long time we can talk about longer support. Ritu nodded slowly.

qa.q: What did Ritu say she just does while everyone else cries?
qa.a: She said she just makes tea.

qa.q: What was Ritu worried about when she came in?
qa.a: Ritu was worried that something was wrong with her because she felt nothing after her brother's death.

qa.q: What did Zubin and Ritu agree to do next?
qa.a: Keep the routines of work, meals and washing up, let feelings come when they come, return next week, and talk about longer support if the heaviness stays.

qa.q: How does Zubin see Ritu's numbness?
qa.a: As a usual reaction in the first days that does not mean Ritu failed to love her brother.

grounding: Feeling nothing after a loss and worrying about it: numbness is common early, keep basic routines, let feelings come, and seek counselling if it stays heavy.

passage: Two weeks after Mridul's father died, the small-town bank branch expected the counter to run as before. Sumit, at the next desk, said, "Good you're back, the files are piling," and slid a stack over without another word. No one mentioned the loss. Mridul stood at the tea stall alone, feeling like furniture. But Mridul told Mrs Pillai, the senior clerk, exactly how heavy the days felt, and she nodded and said, "Ask the manager for lighter work." Mridul did, quietly, and got a few weeks of half-days and no counter duty. Some colleagues still stayed silent, Sumit included. Yet the one honest conversation, and the limit set, made the mornings bearable, and Mridul stopped trying to look normal.

qa.q: What did Sumit say when sliding the stack of files over?
qa.a: Sumit said, "Good you're back, the files are piling."

qa.q: Why did Mridul feel like furniture at the tea stall?
qa.a: No one mentioned the loss, so Mridul felt invisible and unseen in grief.

qa.q: What did Mridul do that made the mornings bearable?
qa.a: Mridul told Mrs Pillai how heavy the days felt, asked the manager for lighter work and got half-days without counter duty.

qa.q: How might Sumit have seen Mridul's return to work?
qa.a: Possibly as a return to normal and time to catch up, or as an awkward moment with no words. The passage does not say what Sumit felt.

grounding: A workplace expects quick return and speaks little of the loss; Mridul feels invisible, tells one trusted colleague and asks for reduced load.
